before: A program is a list of instructions the computer follows. A value is one piece of information, such as the number 30 or the text "coins". Numbers have no quotation marks here. Quotation marks tell JavaScript that the characters inside are text, also called a string. This project uses numbers so it can subtract an amount spent from an amount available.

A variable gives a value a name. In `const savedCoins = 30;`, `const` creates a name that cannot later be assigned a different value. `savedCoins` is the name, and the single equals sign `=` assigns the value on its right. A name cannot contain spaces or begin with a digit. JavaScript distinguishes capital and small letters: `savedCoins` and `savedcoins` are different names. The semicolon ends this instruction.

`console.log()` is a function used to display information. A function is a reusable action; calling it asks it to run. The dot in `console.log` selects the `log` action belonging to `console`. Parentheses `()` contain the value you want to display. Put the variable name inside, without quotes, to display its value. `console.log("coinsLeft")` instead displays the literal word coinsLeft because the quotes make it text.

Assignment and comparison ask different things. `const balance = 22;` assigns a value. `balance === 22` asks whether the value is exactly equal to 22 and produces `true` or `false`. Those are Boolean values, the two possible answers to a yes-or-no question. The minus sign subtracts; the plus sign adds numbers; the star `*` multiplies numbers. Choose the sign that matches the action you mean.

For your project, calculate with the supplied variable names so the calculation follows their values. The supplied amounts give 20 minus 7, which is 13. A second run with spending changed to 5 gives 15. Trace each line: which two values go into the expression, what number comes out, and which name is printed? Storing a number and displaying it are separate steps, and the checks look at both.
after:
A program is a list of instructions the computer follows.

A value is one piece of information, such as `30` or `"coins"`. Quotes mark text, also called a string. Numbers used for calculations do not need quotes.

A variable gives a value a name. In `const savedCoins = 30;`, the name is `savedCoins` and its value is 30.

`=` assigns the value on its right to the name on its left. `const` means you cannot later assign that name a different value.

Names cannot contain spaces or start with a digit. Capital letters matter: `savedCoins` and `savedcoins` are different names. A semicolon ends this instruction.

`console.log` shows information. It is a function: a reusable action you can ask to run.

The dot selects `log` from `console`. Put what you want to show inside the parentheses.

`console.log(coinsLeft)` shows the named value. With quotes, `console.log("coinsLeft")` shows the text coinsLeft instead.

`=` assigns a value. `===` compares values and gives `true` or `false`. These yes-or-no answers are called Booleans.

For calculations, `-` subtracts, `+` adds numbers, and `*` multiplies.

In your project, use `startingCoins - spentCoins` to calculate `remainingCoins`. The supplied 20 and 7 give 13.

Store the result, then print it. If you change the spending to 5 and run again, the result should be 15.
